questions.questionText: Which data structure must Breadth-First Search (BFS) use to guarantee that vertices are explored in non‑decreasing order of distance from the source?
options: Stack (LIFO)
Queue (FIFO)
Priority Queue
Binary Heap
questions.explanation: BFS relies on a FIFO queue so that vertices are dequeued in the same order they were discovered, preserving the invariant that all vertices at distance d are processed before any at distance d+1, ensuring shortest‑path discovery.

questions.questionText: In the BFS traversal described, why is vertex D not enqueued when processing vertex C?
options: Because D has already been visited earlier through B
Because D is not a neighbor of C
Because the queue is full
Because BFS only enqueues vertices at distance 3 or more
questions.correctAnswer: Because D has already been visited earlier through B
questions.explanation: The visited set records that D was discovered via B, so when C examines its neighbors it sees D as already visited and does not enqueue it again, preventing duplicate processing and infinite loops.

questions.questionText: What is the worst‑case time complexity of Breadth‑First Search (BFS) on an undirected graph when the graph is represented with adjacency lists?
options: A. O(V)
B. O(E)
C. O(V + E)
D. O(V * E)
questions.explanation: Each vertex is enqueued and dequeued once (O(V)) and each edge is examined twice via adjacency lists (total O(E)), giving O(V+E).

questions.questionText: What is the primary reason for maintaining a visited boolean array (or hash set) during Breadth‑First Search on a general graph?
options: To record the order in which vertices are discovered
To prevent revisiting vertices and avoid infinite loops caused by cycles
To store each vertex’s distance from the source vertex
To give priority to vertices with a lower degree
questions.correctAnswer: To prevent revisiting vertices and avoid infinite loops caused by cycles
questions.explanation: The visited structure ensures each vertex is processed at most once, which stops the algorithm from looping indefinitely in cycles and from enqueuing the same vertex multiple times.

questions.questionText: In the BFS traversal of the 5‑node graph described, what distance is assigned to vertex E from the source vertex A?
questions.explanation: BFS discovers vertices in order of increasing shortest‑path length from the source. The traversal reaches E after visiting D, which is at distance 2, so E receives distance 3.

questions.questionText: Which statement correctly explains how to ensure that a breadth‑first search visits every vertex in a graph that may consist of multiple disconnected components?
options: A single BFS started from any vertex will eventually visit all vertices, even in separate components.
BFS automatically adds vertices from other components to the queue when the current component is exhausted.
To visit all vertices, BFS must be invoked repeatedly for each vertex that remains unvisited after a previous BFS run.
BFS cannot be applied to disconnected graphs.
questions.correctAnswer: To visit all vertices, BFS must be invoked repeatedly for each vertex that remains unvisited after a previous BFS run.
questions.explanation: A single BFS only reaches vertices in the source's connected component; to cover a disconnected graph you need to start a new BFS from each still‑unvisited vertex.

questions.questionText: During the execution of Breadth‑First Search, which invariant about the contents of the FIFO queue guarantees that vertices are processed in non‑decreasing order of their distance from the source?
options: The queue may contain vertices from any distance levels as long as they were discovered earlier
The queue contains vertices from at most two consecutive distance levels, with all vertices at distance d appearing before any at distance d+1
The queue is ordered by vertex identifier, not by distance
The queue is emptied completely before any newly discovered vertices are enqueued
questions.correctAnswer: The queue contains vertices from at most two consecutive distance levels, with all vertices at distance d appearing before any at distance d+1
questions.explanation: BFS maintains the invariant that the queue holds vertices from at most two successive layers (distance d and d+1). This FIFO ordering ensures vertices are expanded in non‑decreasing distance, yielding shortest‑path guarantees.

questions.questionText: In the BFS example on the 5‑node graph, what is the main purpose of the visited set?
options: It prevents the algorithm from enqueuing the same vertex more than once, avoiding infinite loops and redundant work.
It stores the distance from the source vertex for each node.
It records the order in which vertices are dequeued from the queue.
It sorts the adjacency lists of each vertex alphabetically.
questions.correctAnswer: It prevents the algorithm from enqueuing the same vertex more than once, avoiding infinite loops and redundant work.
questions.explanation: The visited set ensures each vertex is marked once, so BFS does not revisit vertices, which would cause cycles to loop indefinitely or enqueue duplicates.

questions.questionText: What is the overall asymptotic space complexity of a breadth‑first search (BFS) when implemented with an adjacency‑list representation, considering both the queue and the visited array?
options: O(E)
O(V)
O(V+E)
questions.explanation: In the worst case the queue can hold up to all V vertices (e.g., a star graph) and the visited array also stores V boolean flags, giving a total space usage proportional to V.

questions.questionText: In BFS on an unweighted graph, what is the primary purpose of maintaining a visited boolean array (or hash set)?
options: To ensure each vertex is enqueued only once, preventing infinite loops caused by cycles.
To prioritize vertices with smaller degree when expanding the frontier.
To store the distance from the source for each vertex during traversal.
To sort vertices alphabetically before they are processed.
questions.correctAnswer: To ensure each vertex is enqueued only once, preventing infinite loops caused by cycles.
questions.explanation: The visited structure marks vertices that have already been discovered, so they are not enqueued again. This avoids revisiting vertices in cycles and prevents infinite loops or redundant work.
